abstract: This NBER working paper examines early labor market impacts of AI chatbots using Danish adoption surveys linked with administrative labor market records, finding precise null effects on earnings and hours two years after ChatGPT's launch. Despite rapid employer adoption — with most employers in exposed occupations implementing chatbot initiatives — and workers reporting productivity benefits, the study rules out earnings or hours effects larger than 2% at both worker and workplace levels. Rather than wage changes, the primary adjustment mechanism is task reorganization: workers take on new roles in content generation and AI oversight while routine tasks are automated. Some workers transition to higher-paying occupations where AI is more relevant, though insufficient numbers to move average earnings. The findings from Denmark, with its strong labor market institutions, provide important evidence that early AI adoption effects manifest through work reorganization rather than wage or employment changes.
keyFindings: Precise null effects on earnings and recorded hours at both worker and workplace levels, ruling out effects larger than 2% within two years of ChatGPT's launch.
Despite null wage effects, rapid employer adoption occurred with most firms in exposed occupations implementing AI chatbot initiatives and workers reporting productivity benefits.
Task reorganization — not wage changes — characterizes the primary labor market adjustment, with new AI-related tasks (content generation, AI oversight) replacing automated routine tasks.
Some workers transitioned to higher-paying occupations where AI was more relevant, but insufficient numbers to affect average earnings in exposed occupations.
The results demonstrate that early-stage AI adoption effects operate through work restructuring rather than traditional labor market channels of wages and employment levels.
methodology: Large-scale adoption surveys linked to Danish administrative labor market records, enabling precise measurement of earnings and hours at individual and workplace levels. The study uses difference-in-differences estimation comparing AI-exposed versus non-exposed occupations over two years following ChatGPT's launch (November 2022). Administrative data provides exact earnings and hours worked, avoiding self-report bias that affects survey-only studies.
qualifiers: Study is limited to Denmark, which has strong labor market institutions (high unionization, active labor market policies, generous social insurance) that may buffer AI's employment effects — results may not generalize to countries with weaker labor protections. The two-year post-ChatGPT window captures only early adoption effects; longer-term impacts may differ substantially. Danish administrative data is high quality but the labor market is small and structurally different from the U.S. or developing economies. Task reorganization effects, while documented, are harder to quantify precisely than wage and employment changes.
